disguised_difficulty: L5 contains essentially the whole substantive burden of the proof and is stronger than the root theorem's needed claim, because it discards the 2-coloring context and asserts a classification of arbitrary circumcenter-closed subsets of the plane.
fixes_required: Remove or replace L5. Its current statement is false; for example S = Q^2 is a proper circumcenter-closed subset with a noncollinear triple.

Redesign the proof strategy so the main structural step uses hypotheses genuinely available from the 2-coloring setup, rather than the false claim that any nondegenerate circumcenter-closed subset must be all of R^2.
missing_coverage: A correct replacement for L5 is missing. Closure under circumcenters plus one noncollinear triple does not force an arbitrary subset S of R^2 to equal R^2; any valid bridge would need substantially stronger or different hypotheses.
previous_attempt_summaries.strategy_summary: Reduce the coloring statement to a structural theorem about a single color class viewed as a subset of the plane that is closed under taking circumcenters of noncollinear triples. Then prove that some color class must contain a noncollinear triple, and invoke the structural theorem to conclude that this color class is the whole plane.
previous_attempt_summaries.vet_summary: L1-L4 are plausible, but the core structural lemma L5 is false. A proper subset such as Q^2 is closed under circumcenters of noncollinear triples and contains a noncollinear triple, so A4 collapses. The assembly would be valid if all lemmas were true, but the decomposition fatally overstrengthens the needed geometric claim.

domain_restrictions: f is a total function from the Euclidean plane R^2 to the two-element set {red,green}
A,B,C,P,O are points of the Euclidean plane R^2
the hypothesis applies only to triples A,B,C that are noncollinear (hence distinct) so the circumcenter is uniquely defined in R^2
the circumcenter operation circ(A,B,C) is the unique intersection of perpendicular bisectors of AB and AC (uses Euclidean geometry)
root_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every function f: R^2 -> {red,green}, if for all points A,B,C in R^2 that are noncollinear and satisfy f(A)=f(B)=f(C) we have f(circumcenter(A,B,C)) = f(A), then there exists a color c in {red,green} such that for every point P in R^2, f(P)=c. Equivalently: ∀f [(∀A,B,C (noncollinear ∧ f(A)=f(B)=f(C) ⇒ f(circumcenter(A,B,C))=f(A))) ⇒ (∃c ∈ {red,green} ∀P f(P)=c)].
quantifier_order: forall f : R^2 -> {red,green} (consider any 2-coloring of the plane)
assume (hypothesis) forall A,B,C in R^2: if A,B,C are noncollinear and f(A)=f(B)=f(C) then f(circumcenter(A,B,C)) = f(A)
conclude: exists c in {red,green} such that forall P in R^2, f(P) = c

payload.theorem_nl: Suppose that each point in the plane is colored either red or green, subject to the following condition: For every three noncollinear points $A,B,C$ of the same color, the center of the circle passing through $A,B$ and $C$ is also this color. Prove that all points of the plane are the same color.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Fix an arbitrary coloring f satisfying the circumcenter condition, and choose any point O of the plane. First use the basic circumcenter observation on a centered circle: any three same-colored points on one circle centered at O have circumcenter O, so a circle centered at O cannot contain three points of the color opposite to f(O). That is L1. Next invoke the anchored propagation lemma L4, which says that under the given coloring hypothesis, a centered circle with at most two opposite-colored points in fact has none. Combining these, every circle centered at O is monochromatic of color f(O); this is summarized by L6. Finally, if every circle centered at O is monochromatic of color f(O), then every point P is of color f(O), since P lies on such a circle unless P=O, and O already has that color. This is L5. Therefore all points of the plane have a single common color, namely f(O). Since f was arbitrary, the theorem follows.

steps.derives: Fix an arbitrary coloring f satisfying the root hypothesis and fix an arbitrary point O in R^2. For any circle S centered at O, the circle S contains at most two points X with f(X) != f(O).
steps.trivial_justification: Apply L1 to the chosen f and O. If there were three distinct points on S of color opposite to f(O), then since they lie on the same circle centered at O, their circumcenter would be O, forcing f(O) to equal that opposite color. Hence at most two such points can exist.

steps.derives: For the same arbitrary point O and arbitrary circle S centered at O, every point of S has color f(O).
steps.trivial_justification: Step A1 gives exactly the hypothesis needed for L4: the number of points on S with color different from f(O) is at most two. Therefore L4 implies there are actually no such points on S.

steps.derives: For the chosen arbitrary point O, every circle centered at O is monochromatic of color f(O).
steps.trivial_justification: L6 is precisely the universal packaging of the conclusion obtained in A2 for an arbitrary centered circle S. Since S was arbitrary, L6 yields the statement for all circles centered at O.

steps.derives: Every point P in R^2 satisfies f(P)=f(O).
steps.trivial_justification: Apply L5 with the same coloring f and the same point O. Step A3 verifies its hypothesis that every circle centered at O is monochromatic of color f(O). Hence all points P have color f(O).

steps.derives: There exists a color c in {red,green} such that for every point P in R^2, f(P)=c.
steps.trivial_justification: Take c := f(O). Step A4 states exactly that every point P has color f(O)=c.

steps.derives: For every function f : R^2 -> {red,green}, if for all noncollinear A,B,C with f(A)=f(B)=f(C) we have f(circ(A,B,C)) = f(A), then there exists c in {red,green} such that for every point P in R^2, f(P)=c.
steps.trivial_justification: The point O was chosen arbitrarily after fixing an arbitrary coloring f satisfying the hypothesis, so A5 establishes the exact universally quantified root theorem.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let f : R^2 -> {red, green} satisfy the following property: for every noncollinear points A,B,C, if f(A)=f(B)=f(C), then f(circ(A,B,C))=f(A). Fix a point O in R^2. Then for every circle S centered at O, if there exist three distinct points X,Y,Z on S with f(X)=f(Y)=f(Z), necessarily f(O)=f(X). Equivalently: on any circle centered at O, every triple of points of the color opposite to f(O) is impossible.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let O and X be distinct points of the Euclidean plane, and let R_{+}(X) and R_{-}(X) denote the two images of X under rotation about O by +60 degrees and -60 degrees, respectively. Then the circumcenter of the triangle with vertices O, R_{+}(X), R_{-}(X) is exactly X. In particular, O, R_{+}(X), and R_{-}(X) are noncollinear.

candidates.strategy_summary: Unlike the failed attempt, this decomposition does not pass to an arbitrary circumcenter-closed subset of the plane. The key structural step is anchored at a chosen point of the given 2-coloring and uses the full coloring hypothesis on circles centered at that point; this directly addresses the rejected false classification lemma and replaces it by a circle-propagation argument specific to the 2-coloring setup.
